QUESTION ADDRESSED IN THIS BRIEF
Whether the National Voter Registration Act’s ban
on a State’s systematic removal of “the names of ineligible voters” from the voting rolls fewer than 90 days before a federal election (52 U.S.C. §20507(c)(2)(A))
preempts Arizona’s mandate for systematic removals
during that period of persons that officials claim to have
“confirm[ed]” (Ariz. Rev. Stat. §16-165(10)), including by
reference to various databases, are not U.S. citizens.

INTRODUCTION
Congress enacted the National Voter Registration
Act (“NVRA”) to regulate voter registration for federal
elections, after finding that “unfair registration laws and
procedures can have a direct and damaging effect on
voter participation.”  52 U.S.C. §20501(a)(3).  Among the
safeguards Congress enacted, the NVRA prohibits
States from operating most programs “to systematically
remove the names of ineligib le voters from the official
lists of eligible voters” less than 90 days before a regular
federal election.  Id. §20507(c)(2)(A).  Outside this period, States retain wide latitude to systematically remove voters.  States may also remove voters less than
90 days before a federal election, if they do so on an individualized basis.  Congress thus balanced the need for
States to remove ineligible voters with the risk that a
systematic-removal program would ensnare eligible voters, recognizing that any voters wrongly removed close
to an election would likely not be able to correct the error in time to cast a ballot.  In other words, those people
would be denied their fundamental constitutional right
to vote.
Arizona House Bill (“H.B.”) 2243 defies this considered congressional balance, directing precisely what the
90-day provision prohibits: the systematic cancellation of
registrations, including through database matching, of
persons who election officials claim to have “confirm[ed]” are ineligible voters less than 90 days before a
federal election.  The Ninth Circuit recognized that this
part of H.B. 2243 conflicts with and hence is preempted
by the NVRA.  Pet.App.45a-46a.  In doing so, the court
aligned with the Eleventh Circuit’s decision in Arcia v.
Florida Secretary of State , 772 F.3d 1335 (11th Cir.

2

2014), regarding a materially similar database-matching
program.
The Republican National Committee (“RNC”) and
the United States resist this straightforward application
of the 90-day provision.  They do not dispute, however,
that Arizona’s removal program meets each of the statute’s key terms:  It is systematic, its purpose is to cancel
registrations on the ground that registered individuals
are allegedly ineligible to vote, and but for the decisions
below it would operate less than 90 days before a federal
election.  Indeed, the United States concedes (Br.32)
that the plain statutory text encompasses programs targeting persons who election officials claim to have confirmed, including by reference to various databases, are
noncitizens.  Nonetheless, the RNC and the United
States argue that the statute’s words do not mean what
they say.
Specifically, the RNC and the United States contend
that the 90-day provision does not apply to noncitizens
because noncitizens are not (the RNC and the United
States say) “ineligible voters” under the NVRA—even
though noncitizens are ineligible to vote.  In lieu of the
term’s plain meaning, the RNC and the United States
contend that when Congress said “ineligible voters,” it
really meant voters who were once eligible to vote but
are no longer eligible.  To construct their desired meaning, the RNC and the United States employ a convoluted
multistep reading.  But the plain text instead mandates
the commonsense conclusion that noncitizens, who everyone agrees are ineligible to vote, are “ineligible voters” under the statute.  Congress, moreover, plainly
knew how to exempt certain individuals from the 90-day
provision, because it created express exceptions for removals based on an individual’s request, death, criminal
conviction, and mental incapacity, 52 U.S.C.

3

§20507(c)(2)(B).  There is no similar exception for citizenship-based removals, confirming that the RNC’s and the
United States’ atextual demand for such an exception
should be rejected.
Perhaps recognizing this, the RNC and the United
States turn to a consequentialist argument, insisting
that the decision below leaves States powerless to remove noncitizens from their rolls at any time.  That too
is wrong.  The Ninth Circuit’s reading of the 90-day provision in no way bars the remo val of noncitizens, either
on an individual basis at any time or through a systematic program at least 90 days before a federal election.
Under that reading, all Arizona may not do is run a systematic purge of persons who election officials claim to
have “confirm[ed]” are noncitizens (Ariz. Rev. Stat. §16-
165(A)(10)) from its voter rolls less than 90 days before
a federal election.  That prohibition serves the critical
role of protecting eligible Americans from erroneous
last-minute removals that cannot be corrected in time to
avoid denying Americans their fundamental right to
vote.  (Erroneous removals unquestionably occur—far
more frequently than voting by noncitizens, in fact—and
Arizona’s formal requirement to “confirm” noncitizenship before a removal, id., does not foreclose erroneous
removals, especially when “confirm[ation]” is by reference to available databases.)
In fact, the specter of noncitizens who cannot be removed exists only under the RNC’s and the United
States’ reading.  It arises from their premise that an “ineligible voter” for purposes of the 90-day provision must
also be a proper “registrant,” a term found elsewhere in
the NVRA and one that the RNC and the United States
say narrows the scope of “ineligible voters” under the
90-day provision.  The Ninth Circuit did not adopt that
premise.  The RNC and the United States cannot

4

persuasively challenge the decision below by ascribing
consequences that follow only from their (atextual) reading.
Finally, contrary to the RNC’s and the United
States’ contention, the 90-day provision is a limit on the
timing and method of list maintenance, not on who may
vote.  The NVRA leaves States free to set voter qualifications and to enforce them.  And Congress’s judgment
about when bulk removals may proceed falls well within
its constitutional authority to regulate the manner of
federal elections.  Congress drew a line to keep eligible
Americans from losing their fundamental right to vote
due to errors caught too late.  H.B. 2243 crosses that line
and thus is preempted.

STATEMENT
A. Statutory Background
The NVRA regulates both voter registration for federal elections and States’ maintenance of their voterregistration lists.  Of central relevance here, the
NVRA’s 90-day provision provides that “State[s] shall
complete, not later than 90 days prior to the date of a
primary or general election for Federal office, any program the purpose of which is to systematically remove
the names of ineligible voters from the official lists of eligible voters.”  52 U.S.C. §20507(c)(2)(A).  The statute
creates exceptions to this bar for removals based on a
voter’s death, request, or (as provided by state law)
criminal conviction or mental incapacity.  Id.
§20507(c)(2)(B).

10

In 2022, Arizona enacted H.B. 2243, which requires
officials to check available databases periodically for information about citizenship and to cancel the registrations of persons who election officials say they have “confirm[ed],” including by reference to those databases, are
not U.S. citizens.  Ariz . Rev. Stat. §16-165(A)(10); see
also id. §16-165(G)-(K).  More specifically, the law provides that each month (to th e extent practicable), officials must conduct citizenship checks of two categories
of individuals.  Id. §16-165(I).  The first is “federal-only
voters,” meaning Arizonans who registered using the
federal form without submitting documentary evidence
of citizenship, and who under state law are accordingly
registered to vote in federal elections only, see
Pet.App.19a.  The second category is voters who officials
have “reason to believe” are not U.S. citizens.  Ariz. Rev.
Stat. §16-165(I).  The law includes no temporal limitation
on when the prescribed cancellations can occur, meaning
systematic removals can continue fewer than 90 days before a regular federal election.*
B. Procedural Background
The Democratic National Committee (“DNC”) and
the Arizona Democratic Party (“ADP”), along with the
United States, various civic organizations, and Native
American tribes, filed eight lawsuits challenging provisions of H.B. 2243 (and H.B. 2492, see supra n.*)
promptly after the laws’ enactment.  (The cases were
consolidated in the district court as Mi Familia Vota v.
Fontes, No. 22-cv-00509 (D. Ariz.).)  As relevant here,
the DNC and ADP claimed that H.B. 2243 violates the

* Another Arizona statute enacted earlier in 2022, H.B. 2492,
also required removing alleged noncitizens from the rolls.  That provision of H.B. 2492 was superseded by H.B. 2243.  The arguments
herein nevertheless apply equally to both laws.

11

NVRA by allowing—indeed, directing—systematic removals of alleged noncitizens from the voter rolls within
90 days of a federal election.  Pet.App.13a, 15a.
After ruling in plaintiffs’ favor on several issues at
summary judgment and then  conducting a two-week
bench trial, the district court entered final judgment for
plaintiffs on a subset of claims and permanently enjoined
the enforcement of certain provisions, including H.B.
2243’s systematic-removal provisions.  Pet.App.427a-
428a, 431a.
The laws’ defenders appealed.  They asked both the
Ninth Circuit and this Court for a stay pending appeal of
certain portions of the district court’s permanent injunction, but not the bar on systematic removals of noncitizens within the 90-day period.  See Dkt.730 at 1, Mi Familia Vota, 22-cv-00509 (D. Ariz. May 17, 2024);
Pet.App.426a.
After briefing and oral argument, a divided Ninth
Circuit panel upheld the district court’s injunction of the
provisions the DNC and ADP challenged, including the
systematic-removal provision.  The court of appeals held
in pertinent part that H.B. 2243 violates the NVRA to
the extent it “authorizes systematic cancellation of registrations [of persons who officials have supposedly confirmed are noncitizens] within 90 days before a federal
election.”  Pet.App.47a.  Noting both that the NVRA
broadly prohibits “any” program of systematic cancellations from operating during that period, 52 U.S.C.
§20507(c)(2)(A), and the absence of any textual exception related to U.S. citizenship (despite Congress’s inclusion of other exceptions), the court concluded that H.B.
2243’s systematic cancellation scheme—which includes
no pre-election carveout—is “precisely the type of systematic cancellation program that the 90-day Provision

12

was meant to preclude,” Pet.App.46a.  The court also explained that H.B. 2243’s removal program is systematic
because it rests on computerized matching, specifically,
a computer program known as SAVE, for “Systematic
Alien Verification for Entitlements.”  Pet.App.45a (emphasis omitted).
Judge Bumatay dissented from this holding, among
others.  Pet.App.79a, 119a-127a.  The Ninth Circuit subsequently denied rehearing en banc over several dissents.  Pet.App.163a.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
I. The plain text of the 90-day provision encompasses H.B. 2243’s systematic-removal program.  Congress provided in straightforward terms that States
must “complete,” “not later than 90 days prior to the
date” of a federal election, “any program the purpose of
which is to systematically remove the names of ineligible
voters from the official lists of eligible voters.”  52 U.S.C.
§20507(c)(2)(A).  Every element of this provision is satisfied by the mandate in H.B. 2243 that election officials
periodically compare registered voters’ names against
state and federal databases and cancel the registrations
of registered voters supposedly “confirm[ed]”—through
that comparison or otherwise—as noncitizens.  First
(and as no party disputes), the program is systematic,
because it rests on computerized database matching rather than individualized investigation.  Second (and
again as no party disputes), it operates less than 90 days
before a federal election, because H.B. 2243 imposes no
temporal limit on cancellations.  Third, it is a “program”
(no party disputes that either) and thus is covered by the
provision’s reference to “any program.”  And fourth, its
purpose is to remove from the rolls the names of voters
who officials have supposedly “confirm[ed]” (Ariz. Rev.

13

Stat. §16-165(A)(10)), including by reference to various
databases, are ineligible because they are not U.S. citizens.  That such removals are subject to the 90-day provision is confirmed by the provision’s enumerated exceptions, which do not include removals of noncitizens.
II.A. The principal response the RNC and the
United States offer is that noncitizens are not “ineligible
voters” within the meaning of the 90-day provision.  But
that term means exactly what it says: those who are not
eligible to vote.  That, everyone agrees, includes noncitizens.  The RNC’s and the United States’ contrary reading hinges primarily on a term (“registrant”) that does
not even appear in the 90-day provision:  They construe
“registrant” in a different NVRA provision as meaning
only “ properly registered  registrants,” and they then
leap to the conclusion that “ineligible voters” in the 90-
day provision must likewise be limited to “properly registered ineligible voters,” U.S. Br.35, i.e. , people who
were eligible to vote when they registered and later became ineligible.  But the premise of their argument—
that “ineligible voters” under the 90-day provision are a
subset of “registrants”—is baseless; again, “registrant”
is nowhere in the 90-day provision, and nothing in the
NVRA ties the two terms together.  Nor is it hard to
explain why reading “registrant” as implicitly limited to
“properly registered registrants” does not require also
reading “ineligible voters” as implicitly limited to
“properly registered  ineligible voters,” contrary to the
United States’ assertion (Br.39) that “no explanation
[for that distinction] is possible.”  Confining “registrant”
to people who properly attained the status of “registrant” simply limits that term to the genuine instances
of the status it names.  By contrast, confining “ineligible
voters” to people who were once (but are no longer) eligible to vote would not limit the term “ineligible voters”

14

to genuine instances of inelig ibility; to the contrary, it
would exclude the persons “ineligible voters” most obviously describes: those who were never eligible.
B. The Ninth Circuit’s (and the DNC’s and the
ADP’s) reading of the 90-day provision does not immunize noncitizens from removal, as the RNC and the United
States assert.  Indeed, no court applying that reading
has suggested otherwise.  The contrary argument rests
on a non sequitur: that all “ineligible voters” under the
90-day provision must also be “registrants” under 52
U.S.C. §20507(a)(3), which restricts the removal of “registrants” to enumerated circumstances not including citizenship status.  But that is true only under the RNC’s
and the United States’ premise that “ineligible voters”
are a subset of “registrants”—a premise the text does
not support.  The inference does not follow from the ordinary meaning of “ineligible voters,” which is the meaning that the Court should hold Congress intended.
Whether a separate provisio n, §20507(a)(3), permits removing a noncitizen from the rolls is, by contrast, a question about the meaning of  “registrant”—and although
the Court need not construe that term in this case, doing
so to exclude noncitizens (and thereby permitting
noncitizen removal) would be wholly consistent with the
judgment below.
C. The 90-day provision’s use of “any program” is
not a reference to the “general program” §20507(a)(4)
defines and requires.  The latter provision mandates a
single “general program” limited to removals for death
and change of residence, while the 90-day provision
reaches “any program” the purpose of which is systematic removal on any ground.  Congress twice cross-referenced subsection (a)—the subsection that mandates
the “general program”—in subsection (c), but it did not
do so in subsection (c)(2)(A), the 90-day provision itself,

15

which instead refers to “any program.”  The RNC’s
reading would also make the 90-day provision’s exceptions superfluous:  Congress would have had no reason
to make exceptions for removals based on a person’s request, conviction, or incapacity, because the bar would
never have reached such a person in the first place.
D. Prohibiting last-minute systematic removals is
fully consistent with the NVRA’s purposes.  The 90-day
provision exists not to protect ineligible voters (as the
RNC and the United States pervasively say) but to protect eligible voters from erroneous removals discovered
too late to correct without denying Americans their fundamental right to vote.  And Congress had good reason
to extend that protection to people who state or local officials say are noncitizens, as erroneous removals are far
more common than voting by noncitizens.  Nor was it irrational for Congress to exempt from the 90-day bar removals for death or criminal conviction but not alleged
noncitizenship:  Noncitizenship rarely occurs within 90
days of a federal election, whereas convictions and
deaths regularly do so.  At bottom, the RNC and the
United States are simply arguing Congress should have
balanced competing concerns differently.  That is an argument for Congress.
E. There is no merit to amici’s contention that the
DNC’s and the ADP’s reading renders the NVRA unconstitutional (a contention the Court should not entertain in any event because it is raised only by amici).  The
90-day provision does not control who is eligible to vote;
it regulates how federal elections are held, including registration—an authority the Constitution’s Elections
Clause expressly commits to Congress.  And it leaves
States ample means to enforce their citizenship qualifications, both outside the 90-day provision’s window and,
on individualized evidence, within it.

16

ARGUMENT
I. H.B. 2243’S REMOVAL PROGRAM IS PREEMPTED BY
THE NVRA’S 90-DAY PROVISION
The NVRA’s 90-day provision provides in full that:
(A) A State shall complete, not later than 90
days prior to the date of a primary or general
election for Federal office, any program the purpose of which is to systematically remove the
names of ineligible voters from the official lists
of eligible voters.
(B) Subparagraph (A) shall not be construed to
preclude–
(i) the removal of names from official lists of
voters on a basis described in paragraph
(3)(A) or (B) or (4)(A) of subsection (a); or
(ii) correction of registration records pursuant to this chapter.
52 U.S.C. §20507(c)(2).  This provision “strikes a careful
balance:  It permits [individualized removals at any time
and] systematic removal programs at any time except for
the 90 days before an election because that is when the
risk of disfranchising eligible voters is the greatest.”  Arcia, 772 F.3d at 1346.
H.B. 2243’s removal program does precisely what
the 90-day provision was enacted to protect against.  The
law directs county recorders to periodically—monthly if
feasible—compare registered voters’ names against a
series of state and federal databases, and to cancel the
registrations of those supposedly confirmed, through the
database matching or otherwise, as noncitizens, unless a
person, following receipt of a mailed notice, promptly
produces what officials deem satisfactory evidence of

17

U.S. citizenship.  Ariz. Rev. Stat. §16-165(A)(10), (G)-
(K); see Pet.App.44a.  (Those whose registrations are
canceled must also be referred to state and local prosecutors for investigation.  Ariz. Rev. Stat. §16-
165(A)(10).)  A straightforward application of the 90-day
provision makes clear that H.B. 2243 conflicts with Congress’s command and therefore is preempted.
First, H.B. 2243’s removal program is “systematic[],” 52 U.S.C. §20507(c)(2)(A), because it rests on the
computerized comparison of registrants’ names against
other databases—including SAVE, the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements program.  Ariz. Rev.
Stat. §16-165(G)-(K); Pet.App.45a.  Multiple courts have
held that removal programs like H.B. 2243’s, which compare voter-registration databases to other data sources
and use those other sources to cancel registrations, are
systematic programs under the NVRA.  E.g., Arcia, 772
F.3d at 1344-1345; North Carolina State Conference of
NAACP v. Bipartisan Board of Elections & Ethics Enforcement, 2018 WL 3748172, at *6-7 (M.D.N.C. Aug. 7,
2018); Majority Forward v. Ben Hill County Board of
Elections, 509 F.Supp.3d 1348, 1352, 1354-1355 (M.D. Ga.
2020).  No court has held otherwise.
Second, because H.B. 2243 does not impose any time
limits on cancellations, its removal program would operate less than “90 days prior to” a federal election, 52
U.S.C. §20507(c)(2)(A).
Third, H.B. 2243’s removal program is covered by
the 90-day provision’s reference to “any program,” 52
U.S.C. §20507(c)(2)(A).  “[T]he word ‘any’ has an expansive meaning, that is, one or some indiscriminately of
whatever kind.”  Ali v. Federal Bureau of Prisons, 552
U.S. 214, 219 (2008) (quotation marks omitted).  Indeed,
this Court has “given effect to this expansive sense of

18

‘any’” in “case after case.”  Home Depot U.S.A., Inc.  v.
Jackson, 587 U.S. 435, 455 (2019) (Alito, J., dissenting)
(citing cases).
Fourth, the purpose of the H.B. 2243 removal program is to remove from the rolls “the names of ineligible
voters,” 52 U.S.C. §20507(c)(2)( A), specifically noncitizens.  That removals for noncitizenship are encompassed
by the 90-day provision is confirmed by the provision’s
enumerated exceptions, which allow systematic removal
“at the request of the registrant”; “as provided by State
law, by reason of criminal conviction or mental incapacity”; or upon “the death of the registrant.”  Id.
§20507(a)(3)-(4), cited in id. §20507(c)(2)(B)(i).  Congress
thus omitted any exception for citizenship-based removals.  That omission is “good evidence” that such removals
are prohibited, Arcia, 772 F.3d at 1345, because if “Congress explicitly enumerates certain exceptions to a general prohibition, additional exceptions are not to be implied, in the absence of evidence of a contrary legislative
intent,” Hillman v. Maretta, 569 U.S. 483, 496 (2013).
Neither the RNC nor the United States disputes the
first or second elements just discussed.  Indeed, the
United States expressly concedes the first element, stating (Br.43) that H.B. 2243 authorizes “[s]ystematic
checks within the 90-day window.”  The RNC and the
United States do dispute the other two elements, but
they dispute the third only by misreading “any program” as confined to a specific program described elsewhere in the NVRA, and the fourth only by misreading
“ineligible voters” to exclude noncitizens.  Those misreadings are discussed in the next section.
One amicus—contradicting the admission just noted
from the United States—disputes the first element: that
H.B. 2243’s removal program is systematic.  This Court,

19

however, “do[es] not ordinarily address issues raised
only by amici.”  Kamen v. Kemper Financial Services,
Inc., 500 U.S. 90, 97 n.4 (1991), quoted in United Student
Aid Funds, Inc. v. Espinosa, 559 U.S. 260, 267 n.4 (2010);
accord United Parcel Service, Inc. v. Mitchell, 451 U.S.
56, 60 n.2 (1981).  In any event, this argument fails.  The
American Center for Law & Justice (“ACLJ”) contends
(Br.16) that H.B. 2243 “does not remove registrants in
batches” but “requires an individualized investigation of
each potentially ineligible registrant.”  But every systematic program ultimately yields a list of “individuals”
for removal.  To place such removals outside the scope of
the 90-day provision would render the provision a nullity.  And as ACLJ admits (Br.17), a program is systematic for these purposes when it “depend[s] on a mass
comparison of voter-registration records against other
databases, rather than on particularized evidence or an
individualized investigation into each registrant’s eligibility.”  As explained (and as  ACLJ never denies), that
is what H.B. 2243 directs.  Nor does the H.B. 2243 noticeand-cure period on which ACLJ relies (Br.18) change the
analysis.  As the Ninth Circuit explained, a notice issues
“only after the systematic comparison prompts the mailing, as opposed to it being prompted by an individualized
investigation,” Pet.App.45a.
In sum, because H.B. 2243 directs state officials to
systematically remove the names of alleged noncitizens
from voter rolls within the 90 days before a federal election, it violates and thus is preempted by the NVRA’s
90-day provision.

20

II. THE ARGUMENTS OFFERED BY THE RNC AND THE
UNITED STATES ARE MERITLESS
A. Noncitizens Are “Ineligible Voters”
The RNC and the United States argue that the 90-
day provision does not apply to the removal of people
from the voting rolls based on supposed noncitizenship.
It does not apply, they say, because even though no one
disputes that noncitizens are ineligible to vote, noncitizens are nonetheless not “ineligible voters” within the
meaning of the provision.  RNC Br.41; U.S. Br.32-33.
That is not correct.
Indeed, as a matter of plain text—which is of course
the starting point in any statutory analysis—the United
States concedes (Br.32) that “[o]f course, in isolation, the
term ‘ineligible voter’ could describe noncitizens.”  To
reach their preferred conclusion, therefore, the RNC
and the United States must impose an atextual limitation, contending that “ineligible voters” describes only
those presently ineligible voters who were eligible to
vote at some point in the past.  Thus, on their account,
the 90-day provision does not apply to the removal of
noncitizens “who never should have been on the voter
rolls in the first place.”  RNC Br.41-42; see also  U.S.
Br.33.
Notably, even this limitation of “ineligible voters”
would not permit the systematic removal of all noncitizens during the 90 days before a federal election, because some noncitizens—those who were denaturalized
or renounced their U.S. citizenship—were once eligible
to vote.  See Arcia, 772 F.3d at 1348.  In the other direction, U.S. citizens may have been ineligible at the time of
registration because they never actually resided in a jurisdiction.  Thus, the RNC’s and the United States’ reading would implausibly make the lawfulness of last-

21

minute purges turn on distinctions (between noncitizens
who were once eligible and noncitizens who never were,
and between nonresidents who once resided in a jurisdiction and those who did not) that have no apparent justification and that election officials could not apply without ascertaining facts from years or decades earlier.
That would be a surprising distinction for the NVRA to
draw, and the statute does not in fact draw it.  The DNC
and the ADP explained this at the petition stage (BIO
13), yet neither the RNC nor the United States even
acknowledges the point, much less addresses it.  The arguments they offer instead for their unnatural reading
of “ineligible voters” lack merit.
1. The RNC contends (Br.42) that noncitizens are
not “ineligible voters” under the 90-day provision because they were not eligible to vote when they were registered and hence are not valid “voters,” meaning they
cannot be “ineligible voters” (or any other kind of
“voter”).  But that reading renders the word “ineligible”
superfluous; the 90-day provision would have the same
meaning if “ineligible” were omitted.  That superfluity
confirms that the reading is wrong, because courts must
“give effect, if possible, to every clause and word of a
statute,” Advocate Health Care Network  v. Stapleton ,
581 U.S. 468, 478 (2017).  The proper reading, which
gives effect to every word Congress used in the provision, is that “ineligible voters” means all people who are
not eligible to vote at the time of removal, whether or
not they were eligible at some time in the past (such as
when they were first registered).  That is the natural
meaning of “ineligible voters” as again even the United
States concedes (Br.32).
2. Forced to search for support outside the 90-day
provision, the RNC (Br.42-46) and the United States
(Br.33-36) resort to a multi-step argument under which

22

the term “ineligible voters” is implicitly limited to a subset of the “registrants” described in a different provision.  This argument is remarkably convoluted:  Judge
Bumatay, for example, needed five pages—and a
flowchart—just to explain it.  Pet.App.120a-125a.  But in
brief, the reading is as follows:  First, a person who successfully registers to vote is nonetheless not a “registrant” for purposes of the section containing the 90-day
provision, 52 U.S.C. §20507, unless the person was actually eligible to vote when registering.  Second, “registrants” comprise both “eligible voters” and “ineligible
voters,” with the latter being those who were eligible
when they were registered (otherwise they wouldn’t be
“registrants”) but later became ineligible.  Third , when
the 90-day provision bans last-minute systematic removals of “ineligible voters,” it is therefore not talking about
people who were ineligible to vote when they registered;
those people, again, are assertedly not “registrants” and
hence cannot be “ineligible voters.”  Rather, “ineligible
voters” denotes only people who were eligible then but
later became ineligible, for instance following a conviction or renunciation of their U.S. citizenship.
At the petition stage, the RNC sought to excuse the
convolutedness of its argument by asserting that applying “the ‘traditional tools’ of construction” to a “complex
super structure” like the NVRA “requires some explaining.”  Cert. Reply 12.  That is unavailing.  As this Court
has explained, “[w]hen the words of a statute are unambiguous,” the “judicial inquiry is complete.”  Connecticut
National Bank v. Germain , 503 U.S. 249, 254 (1992).
Nothing about “ineligible voters” is ambiguous.  And
nothing in the statute limits “ineligible voters” to those
who were eligible at the time they registered—understandably so, as that would re quire election officials to
ascertain facts about people  from years or decades

23

earlier.  What took Judge Bumatay five pages and a
flowchart to explain was not the statute, but the tortuous reading required to reach the outcome that the RNC
and the United States now espouse.
Notably, neither the RNC nor the United States contends that the NVRA actually says any part of their
reading.  To the contrary, the United States acknowledges that its reading depends on construing “ineligible
voters” as “implicitly limited to properly registered ineligible voters,” even though the term “carr[ies] no express modifier” to that effect.  Br.35, 39 (emphasis altered).  That implicit limitation rests on the RNC’s and
the United States’ assumption that the “ineligible voters” mentioned in the 90-day provision are a subset of
their narrow construction of “registrant[s]” described in
§20507(a)(3)—that is, that only such “registrant[s]” may
be “ineligible voters.”
That assumption is the crux of their position.  But
there is no basis for it.  Th e use of “ineligible voters” to
describe some “registrant[s]” in one part of the NVRA
(§20507(a)(4)) does not mean that all “ineligible voters”
anywhere in the NVRA must be “registrant[s].”  This is
the “fallacy of composition,” i.e., that because something
is true of some members of a group, it must be true of all
group members.  Fallacies of Composition/Division ,
Oxford Dictionary of Philosophy (3d ed. 2016).  Here,
what makes a “registrant” an “ineligible voter[]” is that
she does not meet a state eligibility criterion.  See  52
U.S.C. §20507(a)(4).  An individual who never met an eligibility criterion is no less an “ineligible voter.”  That
“ordinary meaning” is the correct one, Wisconsin Central Limited v. United States, 585 U.S. 274, 277 (2018),
because nothing in the NVRA requires (or even suggests) departing from it.

24

In fact, if all “ineligible voters” were “registrants,” as
the RNC and the United St ates narrowly cabin that
term, then §20507(c)(2)(B)(i) would make little sense, as
it exempts from the 90-day bar three of the four grounds
on which the general-removal provision permits removing a registrant—request, criminal conviction or mental
incapacity, and death—leaving only change of residence.
52 U.S.C. §20507(a)(3).  Congress knew how to denote
registrants ineligible by reason of a change in residence
where it intended that narrow category.  See id.
§20507(a)(4)(B).  General application of the 90-day provision to “ineligible voters” confirms a broader definition.
3. Evidently recognizing this, the United States
speculates (Br.40) that it was some sort of legislative
compromise for Congress to amend the previously unqualified removal ban with exceptions “nearly covering
the waterfront of proper registrants,” rather than enact
“a wholesale rewrite to target only those registrants
who later moved,” even though the latter is what Congress actually meant.  But while it is plausible that adding exceptions to the bar was a compromise balancing
election-integrity concerns with concern about erroneous removals, it is not plausible—and there is no basis to
surmise—that there was any compromise to surreptitiously transform a broad bar into one reaching a single
ground, or to silently exclude from the bar’s protection
all persons who were improperly registered.  Even putting aside that there is no evidence of any such compromise in the extensive legislative history, the United
States’ reading is untenable because Congress “does not
hide elephants in mouseholes by alter[ing] the fundamental details of a regulatory scheme in vague terms or
ancillary provisions,” Sackett v. EPA, 598 U.S. 651, 677
(2023) (quotation marks omitted).

25

The United States alternatively speculates (Br.40-
41) that drafting the 90-day bar as a general prohibition
qualified by enumerated exceptions might have
“serve[d] a distinct function” in that if Congress had instead drafted the bar to reach only registrants who
changed residence, any later expansion of the grounds
for removing registrants would have required amending
the bar as well.  But it offers no evidence that Congress
had any such design, and it ultimately claims (Br.41) only
that its account is “at least as plausible” as the DNC’s
and ADP’s.  An inference that is merely as plausible as
the alternative cannot justify departing from what Congress actually wrote—which was “ineligible voters,” not
“properly registered voters who later became ineligible.”
4. The RNC and the United States next seek support from the label Congress attached to the voter rolls.
In particular, they argue that because §20507 uses the
term “official lists of eligible voters,” a person who appears on such a list must have been eligible to vote when
she was added.  RNC Br.48; U.S. Br.33.  This argument,
in other words, assumes that the “official list[] of eligible
voters” does not contain people who improperly registered to vote because they were “ineligible voters” at
the time of registration.  But it is obviously possible for
ineligible applicants to be registered mistakenly and appear on the “official list[] of eligible voters.”  Indeed, the
whole premise of H.B. 2243 (and of the RNC’s and the
United States’ position) is that noncitizens have in fact
been registered and appear on Arizona’s rolls.  The
NVRA itself even refers to “ineligible voters” who appear on the “official lists of eligible voters.”  52 U.S.C.
§20507(a)(4).  The latter phrase is thus simply a label for
the roll as it exists, not an  impossible warranty about
everyone whose name appears on it.

26

5. The United States’ hypothetical about a university policy barring “any person ineligible to play at a
game” from riding the team bus (Br.37) does not show
otherwise.  The hypothetical shows only what no one disputes: that a general term can carry an unstated limitation.  But the hypothetical’s limitation is not the one the
United States needs.  A coach could board the bus under
the hypothetical policy not because she was once eligible
to play and later lost that status, but because she is not
a candidate to play at all; eligibility to play is simply not
a category that describes her relationship to the game.
Registered noncitizens are not in that position.  They are
on the voter rolls—again, that is the premise of H.B.
2243—and the only reason anyone speaks of them here
is that, despite appearing on the rolls, they are not eligible to vote.  The apt comparison is thus a player who is
listed on the team’s roster but never enrolled at the university.  No one would say that that player is allowed to
ride the bus under a policy barring “any person ineligible
to play at a game.”  Yet that is what the United States’
argument requires.
6. Equally unavailing is the United States’ objection (Br.39) that the DNC and the ADP “provide no explanation why ‘registrant’” in 52 U.S.C. §20507(a)(3) “is
implicitly limited to properly registered registrants, but
‘ineligible voter’ in the 90-day bar should not likewise be
implicitly limited to properly registered ineligible voters.”  The (obvious) explanation is that the two asserted
limitations are not alike—which is why the DNC and the
ADP need not dispute the RNC’s and the United States’
reading of “registrant” in other provisions of the NVRA
in order to prevail on the meaning of “ineligible voters.”
The limitation the RNC and the United States apply to
“registrant” would simply confine that term to people
who were properly qualified to be registered—that is, to

27

the genuine instances of the status the word names.
That limitation, moreover, might be drawn from language in the subsection where the word “registrant” appears:  Section 20507(a)(1) directs States to “ensure that
any eligible applicant is registered to vote” upon the
timely submission of a “valid  voter registration form”
(emphases added).  But the limitation the RNC and the
United States ask this Court to read into “ineligible voters” is entirely different.  It does not confine “ineligible
voters” to those who are genuinely ineligible to vote.  To
the contrary, it excludes from “ineligible voters” the
very persons the phrase most obviously describes: those
who were never eligible to vote.  And nothing in the
neighboring provisions supplies the limitation; the RNC
and the United States instead infer it from their narrow
reading of “registrant,” a term the 90-day provision does
not use.
7. Finally, the RNC argues (Br.46) that “ineligible
voters” must be read narrowly because Congress used
different language in §20507(b)(2), which bars a state
program from removing “the name of any person … by
reason of the person’s failure to vote” (emphasis added).
But the difference in wording reflects the different work
the two provisions do.  Section 20507(b)(2) protects
every name on the roll—without consideration of eligibility to vote—against removal on a single forbidden
ground.  Congress could not have keyed that protection
to “ineligible voters” without excluding the very people
it most obviously exists to protect: eligible voters who
did not vote.  The 90-day provision, by contrast, identifies the programs States must complete by reference to
their purpose, that purpose being to remove ineligible
voters.  Describing that purpose as the removal of “persons,” as the RNC suggests Congress could have done,
would have made the purpose unintelligible.  Describing

28

the purpose as the removal of “ineligible persons” likewise would not have made sense, as it would have left
unstated the respect in which those persons are ineligible; “voters” is the word that makes the meaning clear.
That the phrase fixes what a person is ineligible for—
voting—says nothing about when she became so.
B. The Ninth Circuit’s Reading Of The 90-Day
Provision Does Not Immunize Noncitizens
From Removal
The RNC and the United States contend that the
Ninth Circuit’s reading of the 90-day provision would
immunize noncitizens from removal altogether:  If
noncitizens are “ineligible voters,” they say (RNC Br.51;
U.S. Br.4, 33-35), then noncitizens must be “registrants”
too, and the general-removal provision—which contains
no time limit—would forbid removing them from the
rolls not merely within 90 days of an election but at any
time.  That is incorrect.
The argument’s key step is, again, saying that if
noncitizens are “ineligible voters” then they must also be
“registrants,” such that, under subsection (a)(3), they
can be removed from voter rolls only by request or by
reason of criminal conviction, mental incapacity, death,
or change in residence.  But that is true only under the
RNC’s and the United States’ assumption that “ineligible voters” are by definition a subset of “registrants.”
There is no reason, however, to tie those terms together.
Neither the RNC nor the United States (nor Judge
Bumatay) identifies anything in the NVRA that makes
a person’s status as a “registrant” a precondition to being an “ineligible voter.”  They simply assume the link
and then attribute to the DNC and the ADP a consequence that follows only from that assumption—an

29

assumption the DNC and the ADP reject, as did the
Ninth Circuit.
The Eleventh Circuit has rejected this same argument.  In Arcia , Florida likewise asserted that “either
non-citizens may be excluded at any time, or not at all.”
772 F.3d at 1346.  The court disagreed, explaining that it
was “not convinced … that the Secretary’s perceived
need for an equitable exception” in the general-removal
provision, which prohibits States from removing “registrants” from official voter rolls except for certain enumerated reasons, “also requires us to find the same exception in the 90 Day Provision.”  Id. at 1346-1347.  The
United States characterizes that rejection (Br.38) as a
concession that an “equitable exception” is needed.  That
is wrong; the court simply declined to decide a question
the case did not present.  And on the question the case
did present, Arcia rejected the premise on which the
RNC and the United States rely: “that the NVRA distinguishes between the removals of registered voters
who become ineligible to vote and registrants who were
never eligible in the first place.”  772 F.3d at 1348.
C. The 90-Day Provision’s Reference To “Any
Program” Is Not Limited To The “General Program” Required By §20507(a)(4)
The RNC contends (Br.47) that when the NVRA instructs States to complete “any program” by 90 days before a federal election, it is referring only to the “general
program” described in §20507(a)(4), i.e., the NVRA’s requirement that every State “conduct a general program
that makes a reasonable effort to remove the names of
ineligible voters from the o fficial lists of eligible voters
by reason of … death” or “change in … residence.”  On
that reading, the only program a State must finish before the 90-day window is a program to remove voters

30

who have died or moved—meaning that Arizona’s citizenship-based program could operate at any time.
Again, both the statutory text and precedent foreclose
this argument.
Textually, what the 90-day provision says States
must complete within 90 days of a federal election is not
the “general program” required in §20507(a)(4), but “any
program” for systematically removing voters.  “[A]ny”
such program is a description far broader than the “general program” specified in §20507(a)(4).  The latter involves removals only for one of two specific reasons
(death or relocation of a voter); the former encompasses
systematic removals for any reason.  The RNC’s argument ignores these textual differences, no doubt because
this Court has made clear that “when the legislature
uses certain language in one part of the statute and different language in another, the court assumes different
meanings were intended,” Roberts v. Sea-Land Services,
Inc., 566 U.S. 93, 102 n.5 (2012).
That presumption is nigh-conclusive here because
subsection (c)—which contains the 90-day provision—
does cite subsection (a), which contains the general-program provision.  Indeed, it does so twice, and one of the
two is a cite in the 90-day provision itself:  The provision
states that its ban on 90-day removals does not bar
death-based removals as “described in paragraph …
(4)(A) of subsection (a)”—the general-program provision.  See also 52 U.S.C. §20507(c)(1) (“A State may meet
the requirement of subsection (a)(4) by ….”).  This Court
has deemed similar circumstances to foreclose an argument like the RNC’s, rejecting a request to read the
words “act or omission” into one exception in the Federal Tort Claims Act because “two of the Act’s other exceptions specifically reference an ‘act or omission,’” making it “clear that Congress knew how to specify ‘act or

31

omission’ when it wanted to.”  Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain,
542 U.S. 692, 711 n.9 (2004).  The Ninth Circuit made the
same observation here about the NVRA section at issue,
contrasting §20507(c)(1), which “limits the applicable
program to 52 U.S.C. §20507(a)(4),” with the 90-day provision, which “does not limit the applicable programs to
a specific provision and instead enumerates exceptions.”
Pet.App.42a-43a.
The consequences of the RNC’s reading confirm
that it is wrong.  To start, that reading “offends the
canon against superfluity.”  Roberts, 566 U.S. at 111.  As
noted, the 90-day provision states that it “shall not be
construed to preclude … the removal of names from official lists of voters on a basis described in paragraph
(3)(A) or (B) … of subsection (a)”—that is, removals at
the registrant’s request and removals for criminal conviction or mental incapacity.  Neither is a ground on
which §20507(a)(4) requires a “general program” of removal.  52 U.S.C. §20507(c)(2)(B)(i).  So on the RNC’s
reading, neither would ever have been barred, and Congress had no reason to except either one.
Under that reading, moreover, the 90-day provision
would reach only removals for death and change of residence (because, as noted, those are the only grounds for
removal covered by the general-program provision).
But as explained, the 90-day provision expressly carves
out death-based removals.  See 52 U.S.C.
§20507(c)(2)(B)(i).  Under the RNC’s reading, then, the
phrase “any program” in the 90-day provision would refer only to a program to remove voters who have moved.
The Eleventh Circuit sensibly rejected that interpretation because it “would functionally eviscerate the meaning of the phrase ‘any program’ in the 90 Day Provision.”
Arcia, 772 F.3d at 1348.  “Sur ely when Congress wrote
that the 90 Day Provision applied to ‘any program,’” the

32

court reasoned, “it intended for the provision to apply to
more than just programs aimed at voters who have
moved.”  Id.  “If Congress wanted such a limited result,
it could have said so.”  Id.
Ignoring much of the foregoing, the RNC asserts
(Br.47-48) that the general-program provision and the
90-day provision must “describe the same thing” because they share the phrase “remove the names of ineligible voters from the official lists of eligible voters.”  It
is certainly true that “para llel text” in statutory provisions “counsel[s] in favor of interpreting [those] provisions consistently.”  Lawson v. FMR LLC, 571 U.S. 429,
459 (2014).  But as just explained (and again as the RNC
largely ignores), the relevant text in the provisions here
differs:  One provision says “any program” while the
other refers specifically to one “general program.”  That
the two provisions share other language—because they
address the same general  subject (removals from the
rolls)—cannot erase that key textual difference.
The RNC also notes (Br.47) that the general-program provision directs residence-based removals to proceed “in accordance with” the 90-day provision, 52
U.S.C. §20507(a)(4)(B).  That does not help the RNC.
The language just quoted means that removals under
the general-program provision must comply with
(among other things) the 90-day ban.  That does not limit
the scope of the 90-day provision to the general-program
provision.
Indeed, this language refutes the RNC’s argument.
The language requires residence-based removals to proceed “in accordance with subsections (b), (c), and (d).”  If
that meant that the reference in subsection (c)(2)(A)—
the 90-day provision—to “any program” speaks only to
the general-program provision, it would have to mean

33

the same for subsection (b).  But subsection (b) provides
(with an exception not relevant here) that “[a]ny State
program or activity to protect the integrity of the electoral process by ensuring the maintenance of an accurate
and current voter registration roll … shall not result in
the removal of the name of  any person … by reason of
the person’s failure to vote.”  That would make subsection (b) meaningless:  It would say that “[a]ny State program” regarding removals (a phrase that under the
RNC’s reading means only the general-removal program concerning removals for death or change of residence alone) shall not result in removals based on failure
to vote.
The RNC’s final argument on this point (Br.49) is
that the word “any” “doesn’t expand the kind of ‘program’ covered,” because the term “modified by ‘any’ is
still defined by its ordinary meaning.”  That attacks a
strawman.  The position of the DNC and the ADP is not
that the word “any” changes what a “program” is, but
instead that “any” forecloses interpreting the 90-day
provision to apply to just one program out of the many
possible programs designed to “systematically remove
the names of ineligible voters from the official lists of eligible voters,” 52 U.S.C. §20507(c)(2)(A).
Amicus Advance Colorado presses this same argument by way of legislative history, contending (Br.13)
that the drafting record shows Congress was focused on
address-verification mailings and certain door-to-door
canvasses.  True or not, that history does not narrow the
words Congress enacted.  The Eleventh Circuit recognized this, quoting this Court’s cases in explaining that
its task was “to honor the broad statutory language in
the 90 Day Provision,” because “‘statutory prohibitions
often go beyond the principal evil to cover reasonably
comparable evils,’” and “‘[t]he fact that a statute can be

34

applied in situations not expressly anticipated by Congress does not demonstrate ambiguity.  It demonstrates
breadth.’”  Arcia, 772 F.3d at 1347 (quoting Oncale v.
Sundowner Offshore Services, Inc. , 523 U.S. 75, 79
(1998), and Pennsylvania Department of Corrections v.
Yeskey, 524 U.S. 206, 212 (1998)).  In any event, the enumerated exceptions refute Advance Colorado’s argument:  Congress would have had no occasion to include
the exceptions it did in the 90-day provision (i.e., removals at the registrant’s request or for criminal conviction
or mental incapacity) if the provision reached only address-verification programs.  Advance Colorado ultimately concedes as much, acknowledging (Br.14) that
“[r]esidence is not the only subject of” the 90-day provision.
D. The Ninth Circuit’s Reading Of The 90-Day
Provision Is Consistent With The NVRA’s Purpose
1. The RNC (Br.52) derides the plain-language
reading of the 90-day provision as “‘grant[ing], and then
protect[ing], the franchise of persons not eligible to
vote’” (quoting Bell v. Marinko , 367 F.3d 588, 592 (6th
Cir. 2004)).  That is baseless.  The 90-day provision does
not exist because Congress wanted ineligible people to
vote, any more than the right to confront one’s accusers
or to a jury trial exists to protect the guilty.  Those
rights exist to reduce the ch ances of the government
wrongly convicting the innocent.  Likewise, the 90-day
provision exists to reduce the chance of States wrongly
removing those who are eligible to vote too close to an
election for the voter to learn of the error and correct it,
thereby increasing the risk of denying those Americans
their fundamental right to vote.  And as courts have explained (including the Ninth Circuit here), the 90-day
provision balances the NVRA’s competing purposes

35

“with care,” permitting systematic removal programs at
all times except when “[e]ligible voters removed days or
weeks before Election Day will likely not be able to correct the State’s errors in time to vote.”  Pet.App.46a; accord Arcia, 772 F.3d at 1346.
Congress, moreover, had good reason to extend the
90-day provision’s protection to alleged noncitizens, because erroneous removals (including on citizenship
grounds) are far more common than voting by noncitizens.  As the record here reflects, voting by noncitizens
is exceedingly rare.  Pet.App.227a-229a.  The district
court noted, for example, that there were only “15 indictments for non-citizen voting” during a four-year period
in which “200 million votes were cast in federal elections.”  Pet.App.227a-228a.  (And even an indictment, of
course, does not mean that voting by a noncitizen actually occurred.)  Mistakes regarding registered voters’ eligibility—including based on citizenship—are much
more frequent.  For instance, one district court found
that under Alabama’s citizenship-based program, “more
than 2,000 of the 3,251 voters originally on the list were
inaccurately inactivated,” an error rate “well more than
50 percent.”  Mot. Hr’g Tr. (Dkt.91) at 13, Alabama Coalition for Immigrant Justice  v. Allen , No. 2:24-cv-
01254 (N.D. Ala. Oct. 16, 2024).  Likewise in Virginia Coalition for Immigrant Rights v. Beals, 2024 WL 4601052
(4th Cir. Oct. 27, 2024), the Fourth Circuit recounted the
district court’s finding there that “eligible citizens …
have had their registrations canceled and were unaware
that this was even so,” id. at *2 (subsequent history
omitted).  As the Eleventh Circuit put it in Arcia, then,
the identification of noncitizens for removal is “far from
perfect.”  772 F.3d at 1339.
A recent federal effort stark ly illustrates the point.
In July, the Department of Homeland Security informed

36

Nevada that a systematic review of the State’s voterregistration records “revealed that there may be as
many as 15,903 non-citizens registered to vote in Nevada,” including 8,576 registrants whose “name, date of
birth, address and Social Security number match a noncitizen in our files.”  Letter from Markwayne Mullin,
Secretary of Homeland Security, to Francisco Aguilar,
Nevada Secretary of State (July 16, 2026).  But after
manual review, the number DHS claimed to have confirmed as noncitizens cratered, plummeting all the way
to 185—barely two percent of the original number alleged.  Corasaniti, From 16,000 to 185 to Zero: Trump’s
Claims of Illegal Voting in Nevada Fizzle , N.Y. Times
(Sept. 24, 2026).  Then, when Nevada election officials
examined those 185 registrations individually, they reported that their records showed every one of those individuals to be a citizen.  Id.   Had Arizona officials conducted a similarly botched systematic review, they
would have removed many thousands of eligible Americans from the rolls.  And had that happened within the
90 days before a federal election, as the RNC and the
United States say the NVRA permits, some of those
thousands of voters likely would not have learned of and
been able to correct Arizona’s mistake in time to avoid
losing their fundamental right to vote in that election.
Indeed, without the 90-day provision, Arizona would be
free to conduct that purge after the registration deadline, all but ensuring eligible voters would be disenfranchised.
2. The RNC and the United States tellingly dispute none of this—which is enough to reject their position.  Instead, echoing Judge Bumatay’s dissent
(Pet.App.126a-127a), the RNC says (Br.48) that it would
be “strange” for the 90-day provision to bar last-minute
removal for mistaken or fraudulent registration while

37

permitting it for death, criminal conviction, and incapacity.  The United States similarly contends (Br.36) that
Congress would not have afforded greater protection to
those who were never properly registered.  These arguments fail for three reasons.
First, as Judge Bumatay, the RNC, and the United
States each acknowledge, because legislation often “reflect[s] … compromise,” a law does not “pursue[] its purposes at all costs.”  Pet.App.102a; see also RNC Br.50;
U.S. Br.41.  Hence, it “frustrates rather than effectuates
legislative intent,” Pet.App.102a, to place weight on the
fact that a law could have (in the post-hoc view of a judge
or litigant) achieved its purposes more thoroughly or effectively.  And any argument that a balance different
from the one Congress struck in the 90-day provision
would better serve the NVRA’s purpose is for Congress,
not this Court.
Second, it was entirely sensible for Congress to decide that there is a lower risk of erroneous removals for
death or criminal conviction than for alleged noncitizenship.  The RNC (Br.48) and the United States (Br.42)
each assert that noncitizenship is discerned as reliably
as death or criminal conviction.  But that is wrong, as the
Nevada example just describe d shows clearly.  Death
and conviction are established by a record of the event
itself, a record that (for convictions) follows public proceedings and is embodied in a judicial judgment that is
rarely subject to genuine dispute.  By contrast, noncitizenship is not a discrete event that necessitates the
State recording it in a comparable manner.  Instead, a
person’s noncitizenship is a status that is subject to
change, meaning that a State’s record of a person’s lack
of citizenship can become stale.  Nor is citizenship as
“readily ascertainable” as the United States suggests
(Br.42); indeed, the fact that Arizona law affords notice

38

and an opportunity to respond before canceling for
noncitizenship but not for other reasons, see RNC Br.49,
confirms that citizenship verification is not a simple task.
Third, it was reasonable for Congress to strike a different balance concerning the bases for removal that frequently both arise and trigger removal less than 90 days
before a regular federal election, namely death, criminal
conviction, and adjudication of  mental incapacity.  By
contrast, any change of address arising less than 90 days
before a regular federal election cannot trigger removal
until after the NVRA’s multi-year protective process, so
systematic list maintenance close to an election will not
both catch and remove last-minute movers.  Similarly,
failure to meet initial eligib ility requirements arises at
the time of registration and may typically be addressed
before the 90-day provision goes into effect.  Put another
way, unlike with death, conviction, or adjudication of
mental incapacity, people do not (certainly as far as the
record here shows) regularly become noncitizens within
90 days of a federal election.
3. Congress’s desire to minimize erroneous removals via the 90-day provision confirms that the RNC’s and
the United States’ reading of that provision—excluding
from its coverage anyone who was not eligible at the
time of registration—makes little sense.  Mistakes about
a person’s eligibility (whether citizenship-based or otherwise) can obviously be made both where officials mistakenly think a person was never eligible and where
they mistakenly think the person had been eligible at the
time of registration but later became ineligible.  The
DNC and the ADP made this point at the petition stage
as well (BIO 19), and again the RNC and the United
States do not respond, never explaining why Congress
would have been concerned about erroneous removals
only in the latter situation.

39

The RNC warns, however (Br.51), that on the Ninth
Circuit’s reading, “even when a State discovers a data
error permitting thousands of noncitizens to register—
as New Jersey discovered just last month—the State
couldn’t remove those noncitizens from the rolls.”  Citing
the same example, amicus Center for Election Confidence (“CEC”) adds (Br.24) that “New Jersey could not
correct its errors now, before the November 2026 election.”  Both are incorrect.  The 90-day provision bars
only programs that systematically remove names.  It
does “not bar a state from investigating potential noncitizens and removing them on the basis of individualized
information, even within the 90-day window.”  Arcia, 772
F.3d at 1348; accord Pet.App.43a.  A State that discovers
noncitizens on its rolls on the eve of an election thus is
not powerless; it simply must proceed on more reliable,
individualized evidence rather than by (error-prone)
group purges.  Indeed, that is what occurred in a case
the RNC cites repeatedly (Br.51-52).  See Bell, 367 F.3d
at 590-591.  New Jersey’s experience illustrates the
point:  After learning of the software error that registered people who had indicated they were not citizens,
the State did not simply strike all those people from the
rolls.  Instead, the State referred those with any sign of
eligibility—such as a separate registration or a record of
voting—to county election officials for individualized review, because, as the governor explained, “our initial review indicates that a number of these individuals may be
citizens.”  Statement by Gove rnor Mikie Sherrill (July
28, 2026); see New Jersey Division of Elections, Guide to
MVC Voter Registration Error 2 (Aug. 19, 2026).  Here,
by contrast, nothing in section 16-165 requires individualized review to “confirm[]” that a registered voter is
not a U.S. citizen, Ariz. Rev. Stat. §16-165(A)(10), so
H.B. 2243 invites precisely the kind of pre-election mass

40

removals that the 90-day provision is intended to prevent—rather than the individualized procedures New
Jersey followed.
CEC separately argues (Br.28) that “a hypothetical
citizen wrongly removed from the rolls can generally
cast a provisional ballot and provide proof of citizenship
later.”  But federal provisional-ballot requirements came
into being years after Congress enacted the NVRA, see
52 U.S.C. §21082, so they do not aid interpretation of the
90-day provision.  In any event, CEC’s argument rests
on the dubious assumption that a voter both will
promptly learn of the removal and can get state officials
to fix their mistake quickly enough to have a provisional
ballot included in the count.  That will often not be the
case, and hence, as the Eleventh Circuit explained, voters “removed days or weeks before Election Day will
likely not be able to correct the State’s errors in time to
vote,” Arcia, 772 F.3d at 1346 (emphasis added).  CEC’s
argument also assumes that a provisional ballot is the
equivalent of a regular one.  But provisional ballots are
often rejected when cast by a person who is not properly
registered to vote in the first place, as would be the case
for a person whose registration is canceled through H.B.
2243’s program.  See Provisional Ballots, National Conference of State Legislatures (Apr. 16, 2024).  Moreover,
CEC’s (unstated) assumption that a provisional ballot is
equivalent to a regular one is unwarranted, because a
provisional ballot, unlike a regular one, is counted only if
the voter carries a burden of satisfying election officials’
demand for certain information—information the voter
may not have the opportunity or the money to provide,
much less in the short time frame that is almost invariably involved.  Recognizing all this, courts have treated
relegation to provisional voting as itself a burden warranting relief.  E.g., Majority Forward, 509 F.Supp.3d at

41

1353.  Yet again, the RNC and the United States do not
engage with any of this.
4. In the end, the RNC’s purpose-based argument
reduces to a claim that Congress should have struck a
different balance between the need to remove genuinely
ineligible voters from the rolls and the need not to erroneously remove eligible Americans close to an election.
That, again, is a matter for Congress, not this Court.
And the balance Congress struck leaves States ample
room, as discussed, to keep noncitizens off their voter
rolls.  States may conduct systematic removal programs
at least 90 days before a federal election, and they may
act on individualized evidence at any time.  Pet.App.43a.
The Ninth Circuit’s reading of the 90-day provision thus
“does not in any way handcuff a state from using its resources to ensure that noncitizens are not listed in the
voter rolls.”  Arcia, 772 F.3d at 1348.  All States may not
do is run a systematic purge less than 90 days before a
federal election, when an error is least likely to be caught
and most likely to cost an eligible citizen her vote.  That
is not a flaw in the NVRA’s design; it is the design.
E. The Ninth Circuit’s Reading Of The 90-Day
Provision Does Not Make The NVRA Unconstitutional
No one argued below that the reading of the 90-day
provision the Ninth Circuit embraced renders the provision unconstitutional.  That is dispositive because
“[a]bsent unusual circumstances—none of which is present here—[this Court] will not entertain arguments not
made below.”  OBB Personenverkehr AG  v. Sachs, 577
U.S. 27, 38 (2015) (citing Taylor v. Freeland & Kronz ,
503 U.S. 638, 645-646 (1992)); accord, e.g., Rivers v. Guerrero, 605 U.S. 443, 458 (2025).  A nd even in this Court,
the argument is made only by amici (save for one passing

42

mention in the RNC’s introduction (Br.3)).  That is the
proverbial final nail in the coffin, because this Court, as
explained, does not ordinarily address issues raised only
by amici.  See supra pp.18-19.  There is no reason to make
an exception here, both because of the parties’ failure to
raise the issue below as well as in this Court, see FTC v.
Phoebe Putney Health System, Inc., 568 U.S. 216, 226 n.4
(2013), and because “judging the constitutionality of an
Act of Congress is the gravest and most delicate duty
that this Court is called on to perform,” Northwest Austin Municipal Utility District Number One  v. Holder,
557 U.S. 193, 204 (2009) (quotation marks omitted).
In any event, the constitutional argument fails.  Its
entire premise is that the 90-day provision lets Congress
control “‘ who may vote’” in federal elections.  States
Br.24 (quoting Arizona v. Inter Tribal Council of Arizona, Inc., 570 U.S. 1, 16 (2013)).  But the provision does
no such thing.  It regulates “how  federal elections are
held,” Arizona, 570 U.S. at 16, an authority the Elections
Clause commits to Congress and one that reaches “registration,” id. at 8-9 (citing U.S. Const. art. I, §4, cl. 1).
CONCLUSION
The Ninth Circuit’s decision regarding preemption
by the NVRA’s 90-day provision should be affirmed.
